triage.name: Allergic conjunctivitis
triage.reason: Itchy watery red eyes with seasonal triggers; diagnosis is clinical from history and exam, with good look-alikes (viral, bacterial, dry eye).

demographics: One of the most common eye conditions seen in primary care and pediatrics
Often begins in childhood or adolescence and tends to recur seasonally
More common in people with a personal or family history of atopy

risk_factors.text: Personal history of atopic disease such as allergic rhinitis, asthma or atopic dermatitis
Exposure to indoor allergens such as dust mites, mold or pet dander

chief_complaints.text: My eyes are red and watery
My eyes are watery and runny
My eyes are puffy in the morning

hpi.onset: Gradual over hours to a day, often with a clear seasonal or exposure trigger
hpi.duration: Recurrent episodes lasting days to weeks while the allergen is present
hpi.progression: Symptoms come on with exposure and resolve when the trigger is removed or treated; they recur each season or with repeat exposure
hpi.quality: Intense itching with burning and a gritty or sandy sensation
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; annoying but vision is not affected
hpi.timing: Worse during the allergen season or after contact with the trigger; often worse outdoors and in the morning

associated_symptoms.text: Burning or gritty feeling in the eyes

pertinent_negatives: Sticking shut of the eyelids in the morning
Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts

argues_against: Unilateral red eye with purulent discharge
Severe eye pain with vision change
Fever with sore throat and exudate

positives.text: Wheezing or cough in patients with asthma
Eczema or dry itchy skin in patients with atopic dermatitis

argues_against: Urticaria with angioedema suggesting systemic allergic reaction
Anaphylaxis with hypotension or airway swelling

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not describe itching and instead rub their eyes constantly, blink a lot or appear irritable; parents often notice the eye rubbing.
Symptoms may be milder and overlap with dry eye, so itching is less prominent and burning or grittiness predominates.
Allergic symptoms may worsen or improve with hormonal changes; treatment choices are limited, so symptoms can be more bothersome.
missing_classic_features: Seasonal pattern may be less clear

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; may rub eyes occasionally
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, frequent eye rubbing, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Uncomfortable, constantly rubbing eyes, but not toxic or systemically ill
general.critical: Not applicable; allergic conjunctivitis is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva in natural light
findings.finding: Diffuse conjunctival redness, usually bilateral and symmetric

findings.maneuver: Evert the upper eyelid and inspect the tarsal conjunctiva
findings.finding: Small raised bumps on the tarsal conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tear film and lower fornix
Inspect the skin under the eyes
findings.finding: Dark bluish discoloration under the eyes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower eyelid skin for creases
findings.finding: Extra horizontal crease below the lower eyelid

findings.maneuver: Shine a light into each eye and observe the pupillary response
findings.finding: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a penlight or slit lamp
findings.finding: Cornea is clear without opacity or ulcer

findings.maneuver: Inspect the anterior chamber for depth and clarity
findings.finding: Anterior chamber is deep and clear without cells or flare

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity with a Snellen chart
findings.finding: Visual acuity is normal or at baseline

findings.maneuver: Inspect the discharge for color and consistency
Evert the eyelids and inspect the conjunctival fornices
findings.finding: No foreign body or corneal abrasion

labs.caveat: Peripheral eosinophilia is inconsistent and neither confirms nor excludes allergic conjunctivitis; it is more often seen with atopic keratoconjunctivitis or vernal disease.

initial.why: Not routinely needed; obtained only when a systemic process or another cause of red eye is being considered
initial.only_if: systemic illness, fever, or an alternative diagnosis such as infection is suspected

supporting.why: Identifies the responsible contact allergen in contact blepharoconjunctivitis when a topical product is suspected
supporting.only_if: symptoms persist despite avoidance and a contact allergy is suspected

not_indicated.why: Blood counts are normal in uncomplicated allergic conjunctivitis and do not change management
No role; allergic conjunctivitis is not an infectious or systemic inflammatory process
No role in a clinical diagnosis of ocular allergy
Reserved for suspected bacterial infection, not allergy
Only for suspected infectious keratitis, not allergic conjunctivitis
Not indicated; imaging does not help diagnose allergic conjunctivitis

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical from itching, bilateral redness and watery discharge with a seasonal or exposure trigger; no routine laboratory testing is needed
Red flags such as eye pain, vision loss, photophobia, purulent discharge or contact lens wear should prompt evaluation for keratitis, uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than allergy
Refer to ophthalmology if the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are severe or persistent, or vision is affected

differential.name: Viral conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, watery, bilateral eyes are the hallmark of both conditions, and viral conjunctivitis is the most common cause of acute red eye.

history: Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts
Burning or gritty sensation rather than intense itching
Starts in one eye and spreads to the other over days
Watery discharge without seasonal or allergen trigger
exam: Diffuse conjunctival injection with follicles on the palpebral conjunctiva
Preauricular lymph node may be enlarged and tender
Eyelids may be stuck together in the morning with watery or mucoid discharge
labs: No routine laboratory testing; diagnosis is clinical

differential.name: Bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red eye with discharge is common to both, and bacterial infection is a frequent cause of acute conjunctivitis.

history: Eyelids stuck shut in the morning
labs: Conjunctival culture only if severe, recurrent, or treatment failure

differential.name: Dry eye syndrome
differential.why_considered: Burning, grittiness, and intermittent redness overlap with allergic conjunctivitis, especially in older adults.

history: Symptoms worse with wind, air conditioning, or prolonged screen use
exam: Reduced tear film and tear break-up time

differential.name: Blepharitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid redness, crusting, and irritation can cause a red, uncomfortable eye that may be mistaken for allergy.

history: Burning and foreign body sensation rather than itching
History of rosacea or seborrheic dermatitis
exam: Eyelid margin erythema, scaling, and collarettes

differential.name: Contact lens-related keratitis
differential.why_considered: Contact lens wearers can present with red, irritated eyes, and allergic conjunctivitis is common in this group; missing infectious keratitis risks vision loss.
differential.trigger: Contact lens wear with eye pain, photophobia, or decreased vision

history: Contact lens wear, especially overnight or extended wear
exam: Corneal opacity, infiltrate, or ulcer on slit lamp
labs: Corneal scraping for culture if infectious keratitis suspected

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Red eye with pain and blurred vision can be confused with allergic conjunctivitis, but it is an emergency.
differential.trigger: Severe eye pain with headache, nausea, and halos around lights

history: Sudden onset over minutes to hours

differential.name: Anterior uveitis
differential.why_considered: Red eye with photophobia and pain can be mistaken for allergic conjunctivitis, but uveitis requires prompt treatment.
differential.trigger: Eye pain, photophobia, and decreased vision with ciliary flush

history: Associated autoimmune disease or prior episodes
labs: HLA-B27, ANA, or infectious workup if systemic disease suspected

severity.mild: Mild itching and redness, no impact on daily activities, responds to over-the-counter antihistamine drops or artificial tears
severity.moderate: Persistent itching, redness, and watery discharge that interfere with sleep or school/work; requires prescription topical antihistamine-mast cell stabilizer
severity.severe: Intense itching, marked conjunctival injection, chemosis, and eyelid swelling that limit activity; may require short course of topical corticosteroid under ophthalmology guidance
severity.critical: Not applicable; allergic conjunctivitis is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.meaning: Suggests corneal involvement, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma rather than allergy
Suggests corneal ulcer, uveitis, or other serious ocular disease

red_flags.finding: Contact lens wear with red eye
red_flags.meaning: Suggests infectious keratitis until proven otherwise
Allergic conjunctivitis is typically bilateral; consider other causes

red_flags.finding: Severe headache with nausea and halos

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection
clues: Change from watery to purulent discharge

complications.name: Giant papillary conjunctivitis
clues: Large papillae on upper tarsal conjunctiva

special_populations.differences: Young children may not describe itching and instead rub their eyes constantly, blink excessively, or appear irritable; parents often notice the eye rubbing. Symptoms may be attributed to viral illness or screen time.
Symptoms may be milder and overlap with dry eye, so itching is less prominent and burning or grittiness predominates. Treatment response may be slower.

Allergic symptoms may worsen or improve with hormonal changes; treatment choices are limited, so symptoms can be more bothersome. Avoid systemic decongestants and consult before using new medications.

key_questions.question: Do your eyes itch?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching is the hallmark of allergic conjunctivitis; its absence should make you reconsider the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Is it in one eye or both eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilateral and symmetric; unilateral symptoms suggest infection, foreign body, or another cause

key_questions.question: When did it start, and does it come and go with the seasons or with certain exposures?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes tied to pollen season, pets, dust, or mold; a clear trigger supports allergy

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Clear, watery, or stringy; thick yellow-green purulent discharge suggests bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Is your vision affected, or do you have eye pain or light sensitivity?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in allergic conjunctivitis; pain, photophobia, or vision change suggests keratitis, uveitis, or acute angle-closure glaucoma

key_questions.question: Do you wear contact lenses, and if so, do you sleep in them?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact lens wear with a red painful eye must be treated as infectious keratitis until proven otherwise

key_questions.question: Do you also have sneezing, a runny or stuffy nose, or an itchy nose or throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Concurrent allergic rhinitis supports an atopic cause

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of allergies, asthma, or eczema, or does this run in your family?
key_questions.looking_for: Personal or family atopy raises the likelihood of allergic conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent cold, or is anyone around you sick with red eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent upper respiratory infection or sick contacts points toward viral conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: What have you tried, and does anything make it better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Improvement with cool compresses, artificial tears, or antihistamine drops; worsening with allergen exposure or eye rubbing

key_questions.question: Are your eyelids stuck together when you wake up?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or watery in allergy; thick matting suggests bacterial conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Any new soaps, makeup, eye drops, or contact lens solutions?
key_questions.looking_for: A topical product that could cause contact blepharoconjunctivitis

reasoning_points: Bilateral itchy red watery eyes are the core presentation
Symptoms are recurrent and linked to a seasonal or exposure trigger
Concurrent allergic rhinitis, asthma, or eczema supports an atopic cause
Exam shows diffuse conjunctival injection with papillary reaction and clear watery discharge, with normal visual acuity and no corneal or anterior chamber findings
Red flags such as eye pain, photophobia, vision loss, purulent discharge, or contact lens wear are absent
The diagnosis is clinical, so routine laboratory testing is not needed
Look-alikes such as viral conjunctivitis, bacterial conjunctivitis, dry eye, blepharitis, keratitis, uveitis, and acute angle-closure glaucoma are considered and excluded

easy: Young patient with a clear seasonal pattern and intense bilateral itching
Diffuse bilateral conjunctival injection with watery discharge and normal vision
Symptoms improve with antihistamine eye drops
medium: Perennial symptoms without an obvious seasonal trigger
Older adult with burning and grittiness that overlaps with dry eye
Symptoms that persist despite over-the-counter drops
hard: Contact lens wearer with red eyes where infectious keratitis must be excluded
Patient with eye pain, photophobia, or vision change suggesting uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma
Young child who cannot describe itching and only rubs the eyes
Presentation with purulent discharge that turns out to be bacterial conjunctivitis
Chronic symptoms with large upper tarsal papillae suggesting vernal or giant papillary conjunctivitis
